l: assurance (Ch'i-tiao K'ai's assurance), The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Ch'i-tiao K'ai says that he is not yet able to rest in the assurance of this.

l: Tsze-lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Tsze-lu is portrayed as daring, action-driven, and generous with friends. The Master identifies Yu as Tsze-lu, saying he is fonder of daring but lacks judgment in matters. Tsze-lu may manage military levies in a kingdom of a thousand chariots, though the Master does not affirm his perfect virtue. He fears hearing something new before carrying prior learning into practice. At the Master's side as Chi Lu, he wishes to share chariots, horses, and light fur dresses with friends without displeasure if they spoil them.

l: doctrines, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: make_no_way way The doctrines make no way, according to the Master.

l: raft, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: The raft is proposed as the means by which the Master would float about on the sea, possibly accompanied by Yu.

l: sea, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: The sea is where the Master proposes floating about on a raft.

l: Mang Wu, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Mang Wu asks The Master about Tsze-lu, Ch'iu, and Ch'ih, specifically whether they are perfectly virtuous.

l: Ch'iu, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: might_be_employed_as governor [in a city of a thousand families] Ch'iu might be employed as governor in a city of a thousand families or a clan of a hundred chariots. The Master does not know whether Ch'iu is perfectly virtuous.

l: Ch'ih, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: might_be_employed_to_converse_with visitors and guests [with his sash girt and standing in a court] Ch'ih might be employed to converse with visitors and guests in a court while standing with his sash girt. The Master does not know whether Ch'ih is perfectly virtuous.

s: The Master does not know whether Tsze-lu, Ch'iu, or Ch'ih is perfectly virtuous. Perfect virtue is a standard the Master refuses to affirm for either Tsze-wan or Ch'an Wan because he does not know whether either was perfectly virtuous.

l: Hui, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Hui understands an entire subject after hearing one point, surpassing Tsze-kung in the Master’s comparison.

l: Tsai Yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Tsai Yu is found asleep during the daytime, prompting the Master to compare him to rotten wood and dirty earth. The Master says that Tsai Yu taught him to change how he judges men.

l: Tsai Yu's daytime sleep, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: is_a daytime sleep [Tsai Yu's] Tsai Yu’s daytime sleep leads the Master to say that some people are as unresponsive to correction as rotten wood or dirty earth is to carving or plastering.

l: the Master's change in method, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: is_learned_from Tsai Yu The Master changed from hearing men’s words and giving them credit for their conduct to hearing their words and examining their conduct. He says that Tsai Yu caused him to make this change.

l: firm and unbending man, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: Shan Ch'ang, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: is_influenced_by passions [under the influence of his passions] Shan Ch'ang is identified by someone as a firm and unbending man. The Master says Shan Ch'ang is under the influence of his passions and cannot be pronounced firm and unbending.

l: passions, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: The passions influence Shan Ch'ang, according to the Master. Their influence prevents Shan Ch'ang from being pronounced firm and unbending.

l: man's nature, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: is_discussed_in the Master [discourses that cannot be heard] Discourses about man's nature cannot be heard, according to Tsze-kung.

l: Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: the way of Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: is_discussed_in the Master [discourses that cannot be heard] Discourses about the way of Heaven cannot be heard, according to Tsze-kung.

l: Kung-wan, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: Wan, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: people, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: friendly intercourse, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: Tsze-chang, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: Tsze-wan, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Tsze-wan is a minister who takes office three times without joy and retires three times without displeasure, each time informing the new minister about his government conduct. The Master judges him loyal, while leaving his perfect virtue uncertain.

l: loyalty, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: purity, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: Chi Wan, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Chi Wan thinks three times and then acts.

l: Ning Wu, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: country (Ning Wu's country), The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: little children of the school, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: The little children of the school are ambitious, hasty, accomplished, and complete so far, yet they do not know how to restrict and shape themselves.

s: does_not_keep_in_mind former wickednesses [of men] Po-i did not keep the former wickednesses of men in mind. Consequently, few resentments were directed towards Po-i.

l: Shu-ch'i, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: does_not_keep_in_mind former wickednesses [of men] Shu-ch'i did not keep the former wickednesses of men in mind. Consequently, few resentments were directed towards Shu-ch'i.

l: former wickednesses, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)

l: resentments, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: are_few few [directed towards Po-i and Shu-ch'i] Few resentments were directed towards Po-i and Shu-ch'i because they did not keep the former wickednesses of men in mind.

s: has_neighbor neighbor (Wei-shang Kao's neighbor) Wei-shang Kao is questioned as an example of uprightness. When someone begged vinegar from him, he begged it from a neighbor and gave it to the man.

l: insinuating appearance, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: An insinuating appearance is presented as something of which Tso Ch'iu-ming and the Master are ashamed.

l: excessive respect, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Excessive respect is presented as something of which Tso Ch'iu-ming and the Master are ashamed.

s: conceals resentment [against a person while appearing friendly with him] Friendly conduct is described as appearing friendly while concealing resentment against a person, and this conduct is condemned by Tso Ch'iu-ming and the Master.

l: Yen Yuan, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Yen Yuan says he wishes neither to boast of his excellence nor display his meritorious deeds.

l: wishes, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: The wishes in this unit concern sharing possessions with friends, avoiding boastfulness and display, giving the aged rest, showing sincerity to friends, and treating the young tenderly.

l: one, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: A person has faults but cannot perceive or inwardly accuse himself; the Master says he has not yet seen someone who could.

l: faults, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Faults are described as things that one might perceive and inwardly accuse himself for having.

l: hamlet, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: contains families [ten] A hamlet of ten families may contain one person as honourable and sincere as the Master.

l: one honourable and sincere person, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: An honourable, sincere person may be found in a small hamlet, though less fond of learning than the Master.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: This record summarizes Book VI of The Analects of Confucius, a sequence of sayings and conversations centered on virtue, learning, capable disciples, government, and the superior man. Confucius repeatedly commends particular followers: Yung may be fit to be a prince; Yen Hui uniquely loves learning, avoids transferring anger and repeating faults, sustains virtue and joy amid poverty, and maintains perfect virtue longer than others; Chung-yu, Ts'ze, and Ch'iu can serve in government. He praises humility in Mang Chih-fan, integrity in Tan-t'ai Mieh-ming, and the balance of solid qualities with accomplishments that produces a virtuous person. Encounters with disciples explore practical judgment: Chung-kung distinguishes proper disregard of minor matters from careless ease; Yen Ch'iu is challenged for limiting himself; Tsze-hsia is urged to model the superior rather than mean man; and Tsai Wo learns that a superior man cannot be fooled into folly. The Master also responds to illness and death with grief for Po-niu and remembrance of Hui. His teachings define uprightness, wisdom, perfect virtue, learning, propriety, the Constant Mean, and differing capacities for receiving high subjects. Wisdom means earnestly fulfilling duties toward people while keeping distance from spiritual beings; perfect virtue prioritizes difficulty over success and, at its fullest, establishes and enlarges others as oneself. The book closes with Tsze-kung’s question about one who benefits everyone, leading Confucius to portray such a person as approaching sagehood.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Confucius is presented as a superior man and teacher whose central concern is virtue expressed in conduct, learning, government, and care for others. He helps people in distress without enriching those already rich, appoints and supports officials, and permits Yuan Sze to distribute grain. He assesses disciples and others according to their qualities: Yung may occupy a prince’s place; Yen Hui loves learning and avoids repeated faults; several disciples are fit for government; Mang Chih-fan does not boast. He visits the ill Po-niu with compassion and urges Yen Ch'iu not to limit himself. His teaching distinguishes the superior man from the mean man, urges people to follow proper ways, blend solid qualities with accomplishments, preserve uprightness, and study extensively while observing propriety. He says wisdom is devotion to duties toward people while keeping aloof from spiritual beings, and perfect virtue puts difficulty before success. He also stresses the Constant Mean, though it is rare, and teaches that a perfectly virtuous person establishes and enlarges others as himself. Across the records, he acts as an evaluator, adviser, and moral guide, grounding high virtue in disciplined learning, sound judgment, public service, uprightness, and reciprocal care.

l: Yung, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Yung, praised by Confucius for right words, is portrayed as fit to occupy a prince’s place of authority.

l: Chung-kung, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Chung-kung asks about Tsze-sang Po-tsze. He argues that overlooking small matters is acceptable when joined with reverential attention to business, but excessive when practiced as ease. Chung-kung is the person about whom the Master is speaking in this unit.

l: Tsze-sang Po-tsze, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: does_not_mind small matters Tsze-sang Po-tsze is described by Confucius as someone who may pass because he does not mind small matters.

l: Duke Ai, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Duke Ai asks Confucius which of the disciples loved to learn.

l: Yen Hui, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Yen Hui loved learning, did not transfer anger or repeat faults, and died after a short appointed time.

l: learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Learning is associated with Yen Hui, who loved to learn more than anyone else Confucius had heard of. Learning is studied extensively by the superior man.

l: death of Yen Hui, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Yen Hui’s appointed time was short, and he died. After his death, there was not such another person who loved to learn as he did.

l: Tsze-hwa, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_employed_on mission to Ch'i Tsze-hwa is employed on a mission to Ch'i. While proceeding there, he has fat horses to his carriage and wears light furs.

l: Zan, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Zan, a disciple, requests grain for his mother while Tsze-hwa serves on a mission to Ch'i.

l: Yen, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Yen requests more grain for Zan's mother after the Master assigns her a fu. Yen gives her five ping.

l: Yuan Sze, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Yuan Sze, governor of his town, receives nine hundred measures of grain while Tsze-hwa serves in Ch'i, declines them, and is urged to give them away locally.

l: Ch'i, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Ch'i is Tsze-hwa's mission destination and a state said to be one change away from becoming like Lu.

l: mission to Ch'i, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_to Ch'i The mission to Ch'i employs Tsze-hwa, who proceeds there with fat horses to his carriage and light furs.

l: grain, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Grain is measured in fu, yu, and ping; it is requested for Zan’s mother, assigned, given, and distributed from Yuan Sze’s nine hundred measures.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The superior man helps the distressed without adding to the wealth of the rich. He may be sent to a well and imposed upon, yet cannot be sent down into it or fooled. He extensively studies learning and observes rules of propriety, thereby not overstepping what is right.

l: governorship of a town, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_held_by Yuan Sze The governorship of a town is given to Yuan Sze by the Master.

l: calf, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The calf, offspring of a brindled cow, is red and horned; though men may not wish to use it, the Master questions whether mountain and river spirits would reject it.

l: spirits of the mountains and rivers, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: put_aside calf [despite men not wishing to use it] The spirits of the mountains and rivers are asked whether they would put aside a red and horned calf of a brindled cow that people did not wish to use.

l: Hui, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Hui maintains a mind free from anything contrary to perfect virtue for three months. Living joyfully despite distress in a mean narrow lane, with only a bamboo dish of rice and gourd dish of drink, he is admirable.

l: perfect virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Perfect virtue is a state in which nothing contrary is present in the mind. Hui maintained it for three months. It consists in making difficulty one’s first business, while regarding success only as a subsequent consideration.

l: Chi K'ang, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Chi K'ang asks the Master whether Chung-yu, Ts'ze, and Ch'iu are fit to be employed as officers of government.

l: Chung-yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Chung-yu is a man of decision, judged fit for government office and able to serve as an officer without difficulty.

l: Ts'ze, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Ts'ze is described as intelligent and capable of serving as an officer of government without difficulty.

l: Yen Ch'iu, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Yen Ch'iu is a man of various ability, fit to serve as an officer of government. He delights in the doctrines but says his strength is insufficient; the Master replies that he is limiting himself.

l: fitness for employment as an officer of government, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Chung-yu, Ts'ze, and Ch'iu are each judged fit for employment as officers of government. Their fitness is associated with decision, intelligence, and various ability, respectively.

l: chief of the Chi family, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Chief of the Chi family sends to ask Min Tsze-ch'ien to become governor of Pi.

l: Chi family, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_a family The Chi family is represented by its chief, who sent to ask Min Tsze-ch'ien to be governor of Pi.

l: Min Tsze-ch'ien, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Min Tsze-ch'ien said the offer should be declined politely. He said that if someone came again with a second invitation, he would have to go and live on the banks of the Wan.

l: governor of Pi, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: governs Pi Min Tsze-ch'ien was asked to be governor of Pi.

l: offer, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The offer was for Min Tsze-ch'ien to be governor of Pi, and he said it should be declined politely.

l: invitation, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Min Tsze-ch'ien said that a second invitation would oblige him to go and live on the banks of the Wan.

l: Po-niu, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Po-niu is an ill person whose sickness is killing him; the Master visits and holds his hand through the window.

l: sickness, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Po-niu’s sickness, called an appointment of Heaven, is killing him; the Master visits, laments, and questions why such a man suffers.

l: Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: rejects the Master (Nan-tsze's visitor) [if the Master has done improperly] Heaven was invoked by the Master as the one who should reject him if he had done improperly.

l: virtue of Hui, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_admirable admirable The Master describes the virtue of Hui as admirable. It is shown by Hui’s ability to remain joyful despite poverty and distress.

l: doctrines, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: are_taught_by the Master The doctrines are what Yen Ch'iu says he delights in.

l: strength, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Yen Ch'iu says that his strength is insufficient. The Master connects insufficient strength with giving over in the middle of the way.

l: those whose strength is insufficient, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: give_over in the middle of the way Those whose strength is insufficient give over in the middle of the way.

l: Tsze-hsia, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_told_to_be scholar [after the style of the superior man] Tsze-hsia is told by the Master to be a scholar after the style of the superior man, not the mean man.

l: scholar, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: A scholar is urged by the Master to follow the superior man’s style and reject the mean man’s style.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The superior man provides the style after which the Master tells Tsze-hsia to be a scholar.

l: mean man, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The mean man provides a style after which the Master tells Tsze-hsia not to be a scholar.

l: Tsze-yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Tsze-yu, governor of Wu-ch'ang, tells the Master about Tan-t'ai Mieh-ming when asked about good men there.

l: Wu-ch'ang, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Wu-ch'ang, governed by Tsze-yu, is notable for having good men.

l: Tan-t'ai Mieh-ming, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: A good man in Wu-ch'ang avoids shortcuts and visits Tsze-yu's office only for public business.

l: Mang Chih-fan, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: does_not_boast_of merit Mang Chih-fan does not boast of his merit. During an occasion of flight, he was in the rear and whipped up his horse as they approached the gate, saying that he was not daring to be last but that his horse would not advance.

l: an occasion of flight, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: An occasion of flight involved Mang Chih-fan being in the rear as they approached the gate.

l: horse, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Mang Chih-fan said that his horse would not advance.

l: the present age, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The present age is described as a time when it is difficult to escape without the specious speech of the litanist T'o and the beauty of the prince Chao of Sung.

l: escape, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_difficult difficult [in the present age] Escape is described as difficult in the present age without the specious speech of the litanist T'o and the beauty of the prince Chao of Sung.

l: door, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The door is presented as the means by which one goes out.

l: men, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Men can go out only by the door, yet are described as not walking according to these ways.

l: ways, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The ways are presented as paths according to which men should walk.

l: solid qualities, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Solid qualities, excessive over accomplishments, produce rusticity; equally blended with accomplishments, they contribute to the man of virtue.

l: accomplishments, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Accomplishments, excessive over solid qualities, produce clerkly manners; equally blended with solid qualities, they contribute to the man of virtue.

l: rusticity, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Rusticity results when solid qualities are in excess of accomplishments.

l: manners of a clerk, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The manners of a clerk result when accomplishments are in excess of solid qualities.

l: man of virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The man of virtue results from an equal blending of accomplishments and solid qualities. His perfect virtue follows the Constant Mean, though such practice has long been rare among the people. He first prioritizes overcoming difficulty and treats success afterward. Virtue unfolds through establishing and enlarging oneself and others, and through judging others by what is near in oneself.

l: man, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_born_for uprightness Man is born for uprightness. If a man loses his uprightness and still lives, his survival is attributed to mere good fortune.

l: uprightness, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Uprightness is what man is born for. Losing uprightness while continuing to live is presented as an abnormal condition dependent on good fortune.

l: escape from death, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: is_effect_of good fortune [mere] Escape from death, when a man has lost his uprightness but continues living, is the effect of mere good fortune.

l: death, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Death is the danger from which a man may escape after losing his uprightness. Such an escape is described as the result of mere good fortune.

l: good fortune, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Good fortune is identified as the cause of a man's escape from death when he has lost his uprightness yet continues to live.

l: truth, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The truth is known, loved, and delighted in by different people, with these forms of engagement presented as unequal.

l: those who know the truth, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Those who know the truth are not equal to those who love the truth.

l: those who love the truth, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Those who love the truth are distinguished from, and ranked below, those who delight in it.

l: those who delight in the truth, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: delight_in truth Those who delight in the truth are presented as distinct from, and beyond, those who love it.

l: those whose talents are above mediocrity, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The Master says those whose talents are above mediocrity may be told the highest subjects.

l: those who are below mediocrity, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The Master distinguishes those below mediocrity from those above, withholding the highest subjects from the former.

l: the highest subjects, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: They may be announced to those whose talents are above mediocrity, but not to those who are below mediocrity.

l: Fan Ch'ih, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Fan Ch'ih asks the Master what constitutes wisdom and perfect virtue.

l: wisdom, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Wisdom consists in earnest devotion to duties due to people, while respecting spiritual beings yet keeping aloof from them.

l: the wise, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The wise find pleasure in water and are active and joyful.

l: the virtuous, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The virtuous find pleasure in hills; they are tranquil and long-lived.

l: water, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Water is associated with the pleasure of the wise.

l: hills, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Hills are associated with the pleasure of the virtuous.

l: Lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: comes_to a State where true principles predominated [by one change] Lu would come to a State where true principles predominated by one change.

l: change, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: One change would bring Ch'i to the State of Lu and would bring Lu to a State where true principles predominated.

l: a State where true principles predominated, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: has_predominating true principles It is the state that Lu would come to by one change.

l: true principles, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: True principles predominated in the state that Lu would come to by one change.

l: cornered vessel, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: A strange cornered vessel is described from beginning to end as having no corners.

l: Tsai Wo, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Tsai Wo asks Confucius whether a benevolent man would go into a well after being told that someone was in it.

l: benevolent man, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The benevolent man is presented as someone who might be told that a man is in the well and questioned about whether he would go in after him.

l: well, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The well is the place where a man is said to be, and a superior man may be made to go to it but cannot be made to go down into it.

l: rules of propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The rules of propriety restrain the superior man and help him avoid overstepping what is right.

l: Nan-tsze, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Nan-tsze was visited by the Master.

l: Tsze-lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Tsze-lu was displeased after the Master visited Nan-tsze.

l: the Master's visit to Nan-tsze, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The Master visits Nan-tsze, and the visit causes Tsze-lu to be displeased.

l: Tsze-lu's displeasure, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Tsze-lu's displeasure follows the Master's visit to Nan-tsze and leads the Master to swear.

l: the Master's oath, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The Master's oath, following his visit to Nan-tsze, calls on Heaven to reject him if he acted improperly.

l: Constant Mean, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The Constant Mean is presented as the standard according to which perfect virtue is practiced.

l: Tsze-kung, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: Tsze-kung asks the Master whether a man who extensively benefits the people and assists all could be called perfectly virtuous.

l: man (Tsze-kung's hypothetical case), The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: A hypothetical man extensively benefits people and assists all; with perfect virtue, he establishes and enlarges others as himself, unfolding into one the Master says has a sage’s qualities.

l: the people, The Analects of Confucius, Book VI (Yung Yey)
s: The people are the recipients of the hypothetical man's extensive benefits.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book VII (Shu R)
s: This unit presents Confucius's teachings and conduct concerning learning, virtue, propriety, self-discipline, and the superior man. Confucius describes himself as a transmitter who loves antiquity, pursues knowledge, teaches others, and seeks to become virtuous without weariness. He emphasizes selecting and following good qualities, avoiding bad ones, acting with careful planning, and remaining content without unrighteous riches. The unit also records his views on the superior man, whose conduct should match his words and who is composed rather than distressed.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book VII (Shu R)
s: Confucius describes himself as a transmitter rather than a maker, loving antiquity and seeking knowledge there. He teaches without refusing instruction, does not conceal his conduct from his disciples, and strives to become a sage or a man of perfect virtue without satiety.

l: virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book VII (Shu R)
s: Virtue is presented as something requiring cultivation, pursuit, and alignment with action. Confucius says virtue is not remote: when he wishes to be virtuous, it is at hand, and he attributes the virtue in him to Heaven.

l: knowledge, The Analects of Confucius, Book VII (Shu R)
s: Knowledge is silently treasured, pursued through learning without satiety, and shared by instructing others. Confucius says he was not born possessing knowledge; he seeks it in antiquity, hears much, selects what is good, follows it, and retains what he sees.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book VII (Shu R)
s: The superior man carries out in conduct what he professes, a standard Confucius says he has not yet attained. The superior man is satisfied and composed, is not a partisan, and is distinguished from the mean man, who is full of distress.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: The unit presents teachings of Confucius and the philosopher Tsang on virtuous conduct, learning, propriety, government, and personal humility. It describes how the people respond to the conduct of those in high stations and what conditions accompany good or bad government. It praises Shun, Yu, Yao, King Wan, and King Wu for their governance and virtue, while emphasizing the importance of perfect virtue, sincerity, and endurance. The unit concludes that Yu displayed filial piety, elegance in sacrifice, and great labor for the empire despite his simple way of living.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: Confucius says that talents are difficult to find and discusses the ministers of Shun, King Wu, and the dynasties of T'ang, Yu, and Chau. He praises King Wan for serving the dynasty of Yin with two parts of the empire and says that the virtue of the house of Chau reached the highest point.

l: the people, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: The people cannot express their approval of T'ai-po because they do not know his motives. They are aroused to virtue when those in high stations fulfill their duties to their relations, and preserved from meanness when old friends are not neglected. They may be made to follow a path of action but may not be made to understand it.

l: rules of propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: Rules of propriety prevent respectfulness from becoming laborious bustle, carefulness from becoming timidity, boldness from becoming insubordination, and straightforwardness from becoming rudeness. They establish the character.

l: the philosopher Tsang, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: The philosopher Tsang teaches caution, sincerity, proper conduct, and endurance. While ill, he says that a man's words are good when he is about to die, and he praises a person who is able, humble, patient, and unwilling to enter into altercation.

l: a superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: A superior man can be entrusted with a young orphan prince and authority over a state of a hundred li. No emergency, however great, can drive him from his principles.

l: perfect virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: Perfect virtue is described as the burden that an officer considers it his duty to sustain. The burden lasts until death.

l: the Odes, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: The Odes arouse the mind.

l: Music, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: Music gives the finish to a person's development. The finish of the Kwan Tsu is described as magnificent and filling the ears.

l: Shun, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: Shun had five ministers, and the empire was well-governed under him. His manner of holding possession of the empire is described as majestic and as if it were nothing to him.

l: Yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: Yu is praised for having no flaw in his character. He used coarse food and drink, showed the utmost filial piety toward the spirits, wore poor ordinary garments while displaying elegance in his sacrificial cap and apron, and expended all his strength on ditches and water-channels.

l: Yao, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: Yao is praised as a majestic sovereign whose virtue corresponded to the grandeur of Heaven. His virtue was so vast that the people could find no name for it, and he was majestic in his works and glorious in the regulations he instituted.

l: the empire, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: The empire was well-governed when Shun had five ministers. King Wan possessed two of its three parts and used them to serve the dynasty of Yin.

l: right principles of government, The Analects of Confucius, Book VIII (T'ai-po)
s: When right principles of government prevail in the kingdom, a person of sincere faith and love of learning will show himself. When those principles are prostrated, he will keep concealed.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: This unit from Book IX, Tsze Han, presents the Master through sayings, encounters, and the responses of his disciples. He seldom speaks of profitableness, Heaven’s appointments, and perfect virtue, yet he is portrayed as learned, adaptable, ceremonially principled, free of egoism and obstinacy, and confident that Heaven protects the cause of truth entrusted to him. Though praised for many abilities, he attributes them to his low early condition and lack of office, and he denies being inherently knowledgeable, saying instead that he fully explains questions put to him. He shows reverence toward mourners, the formally dressed, and blind people; reforms music after returning from Wei to Lu; and rejects a false display of ministerial attendants during illness. He would sell a beautiful gem only when its price is offered, considers living among eastern tribes, and reflects pessimistically that the FANG bird and river map no longer appear. The Master’s teaching is described as profound and demanding. Yen Yuan finds it ever higher, firmer, and elusive, though taught through orderly method, learning, and propriety. The Master compares learning to building a mound: progress or stopping belongs to the learner. He praises Hui and Yen Yuan for unceasing advancement, while observing that growth does not always reach flowering or fruit. He urges respect for youth, faithfulness and sincerity, abandoning faults, and turning admonition into reformed conduct and gentle advice into clarified purpose. The closing sayings stress inner character: a common person’s will cannot be taken, Yu’s freedom from shame and desire falls short of perfect excellence, pine and cypress endure cold, and the wise, virtuous, and bold are free respectively from perplexity, anxiety, and fear. Companionship in study does not guarantee shared principle, establishment, or judgment. The final image of fluttering aspen-plum flowers concludes that distance comes from want of thought, not from the remoteness of a house.

l: The Analects of Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: translated_by James Legge The Analects of Confucius includes Book IX, Tsze Han, which contains a chapter about subjects the Master seldom spoke of.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Confucius is a philosopher and Master characterized by learning, teaching, humility, ritual attentiveness, and moral demands. Though described as nearly a sage and endowed by Heaven, he says he is not knowledgeable; his low condition when young led him to acquire many arts while without office. When questioned by someone seemingly empty-like, he explains a matter exhaustively. He seldom speaks of profitableness, appointments of Heaven, or perfect virtue, and is entirely free of foregone conclusions, predeterminations, obstinacy, and egoism. He follows economical common practice concerning caps but rejects arrogant practice concerning bowing, continually bowing below the hall. He treats people in mourning, full dress, and blindness with marked respect. As a teacher, he leads through orderly method, enlarges Yen Yuan with learning, and teaches propriety as restraint; he praises Hui for never flagging. His sayings stress persistence in learning, sincerity, reform after admonition, steadfast will, virtue over beauty, and the distinct qualities of the wise, virtuous, and bold. Put in fear in K'wang, he sees himself as bearing the cause of truth after King Wan's death. In illness he rejects a false display of ministers, preferring death among disciples or even on the road. He advises selling a gem when the right buyer appears, wishes to live among eastern tribes, returns from Wei to Lu and reforms music, and reflects by a stream on ceaseless passing. His later sayings warn that promise may not flower or fruit, call for respect toward youth, and insist that distance comes from want of thought.

l: profitableness, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Profitableness is named as a subject about which the Master seldom spoke.

l: appointments of Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The appointments of Heaven are named as a subject about which the Master seldom spoke.

l: perfect virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Perfect virtue is named as a subject about which the Master seldom spoke.

l: man (village of Ta-hsiang), The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: A man from Ta-hsiang calls K'ung great and extensively learned, yet notes no particular achievement makes K'ung's name famous.

l: charioteering, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Charioteering is the practice K'ung chooses when considering whether to practise it or archery.

l: linen cap, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_prescribed_by rules of ceremony The linen cap is prescribed by the rules of ceremony, but it is no longer the common practice.

l: silk cap, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Silk cap is commonly worn instead of the prescribed linen cap because it is economical.

l: rules of ceremony, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: prescribes bowing [below the hall] The rules of ceremony prescribe the linen cap and bowing below the hall.

l: common practice, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: places_bowing_after ascending the hall [only after ascending it] The common practice is to wear a silk cap and to bow only after ascending the hall. The Master follows it for the cap but opposes it for bowing.

l: bowing, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: occurs_below hall [as prescribed by the rules of ceremony] The prescribed practice is to bow below the hall, while the current practice is to bow after ascending it. The Master considers the latter arrogant and continues to bow below the hall.

l: foregone conclusions, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master had no foregone conclusions.

l: arbitrary predeterminations, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master had no arbitrary predeterminations.

l: obstinacy, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master had no obstinacy.

l: egoism, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master had no egoism.

l: K'wang, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master was put in fear in K'wang. He asks what the people of K'wang can do to him while Heaven does not let the cause of truth perish.

l: Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: preserves cause of truth [while Heaven does not let it perish] Heaven is described as having the power to let the cause of truth perish or preserve it. The Master trusts that while Heaven does not let it perish, the people of K'wang cannot harm him.

l: cause of truth, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: lodged_in the Master [after the death of King Wan] After the death of King Wan, the cause of truth was lodged in the Master. The Master says that Heaven has not allowed it to perish.

l: Tsze-kung, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Tsze-kung responds to a high officer that Heaven endowed the Master abundantly, making him nearly a sage with varied ability. Tsze-kung asks whether to keep a beautiful gem in a case or seek a good price and sell it.

l: high officer, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: A high officer asks Tsze-kung whether the Master may be called a sage, pointing to the variety of his ability.

l: a superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: needs variety of ability [does not] A superior man is presented as someone whose presence among the nine wild tribes of the east would eliminate rudeness.

l: sage, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The high officer asks whether the Master is a sage, and Tsze-kung says that he is about a sage.

l: ability, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master’s varied abilities, acquired through mean matters in youth, are discussed; he says a superior man need not possess such variety.

l: knowledge, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master questions whether he possesses knowledge and says that he is not knowing.

l: FANG bird, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: come not coming The FANG bird does not come.

l: person in a mourning dress, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: wears mourning dress The person in a mourning dress is treated with respect by the Master, who rises when observing them approach and passes hastily if necessary.

l: person in full dress, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: wears full dress [including the cap and upper and lower garments] The person in full dress, wearing the cap and upper and lower garments of full dress, is treated with respect by the Master, who rises when observing them approach and passes hastily if necessary.

l: blind person, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The blind person is treated with respect by the Master, who rises when observing them approach and passes hastily if necessary.

l: Yen Yuan, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Yen Yuan admires and studies the Master's doctrines, sighing at their depth. Though difficulty leaves him unable to find how to follow and grasp them, he advances constantly; the Master says he never saw him stop.

l: the Master's doctrines, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master's doctrines appear increasingly high, firm, and elusive to Yen Yuan. They stand before him as something he cannot fully reach or grasp.

l: Tsze-lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Tsze-lu wishes disciples to pose as the Master’s ministers during illness, drawing criticism as deceitful; later he continually recites words praising freedom from dislike and covetousness.

l: disciples, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The disciples are asked by Tsze-lu to act as ministers to the Master. The Master says he would rather die in their hands than in the hands of ministers.

l: ministers, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Ministers are falsely presented as existing for the Master, although he has none. The Master says he would rather die in the hands of his disciples than in the hands of ministers.

l: illness, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The illness makes the Master very ill, though he later experiences a remission.

l: death of the Master, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master says he would rather die in the hands of his disciples than in the hands of ministers. He also says that, even without a great burial, he would accept dying on the road.

l: gem, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_a beautiful gem The gem is described as beautiful and is being considered for storage or sale.

l: price, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: A beautiful gem is sought for sale; Tsze-kung may seek its price, while the Master waits for an offer.

l: selling the gem, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Selling the gem is presented as the preferred course, provided that someone offers the price.

l: the nine wild tribes of the east, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Nine wild tribes in the east are described as rude; the Master wishes to go and live among them.

l: rudeness, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Rudeness is attributed to the nine wild tribes of the east, but the Master says it would not exist if a superior man dwelt among them.

l: Wei, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Wei was the place from which the Master returned.

l: Lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Lu was the place to which the Master returned.

l: return from Wei to Lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The Master returned from Wei to Lu. After this return, the music was reformed.

l: music, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_reformed reformed The music was reformed after the Master returned from Wei to Lu.

l: reformation of the music, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The reformation of the music occurred after the Master returned from Wei to Lu.

l: Royal songs, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The pieces in the Royal songs found their proper places after the music was reformed.

l: Praise songs, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The pieces in the Praise songs found their proper places after the music was reformed.

l: pieces in the Royal songs and Praise songs, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The pieces in Royal songs and Praise songs found their proper places after the music was reformed.

l: stream, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: A stream passes on continuously, never ceasing during either day or night.

l: virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Virtue is described as something that no one has been seen to love as much as beauty.

l: beauty, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Beauty is presented as something loved more than virtue by the person described by the Master.

l: prosecution of learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_compared_to mound [in raising it] The prosecution of learning is compared to raising a mound. Its completion or advancement depends on whether one stops short or continues forward incrementally.

l: Hui, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: has_disposition never flagging [when The Master sets forth anything to him] Hui is described as never flagging when the Master sets forth anything to him.

l: cases, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_a situations Some cases involve the blade springing without the plant going on to flower. Other cases involve flowering without any fruit subsequently being produced.

l: blade, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: springs springs [in some cases] The blade springs in some cases.

l: plant, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The plant may stop before flowering; if it flowers, it may still fail to produce fruit.

l: flowering, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Flowering occurs in some cases, but it is not followed by the production of fruit.

l: fruit, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_produced not subsequently produced [after flowering in some cases] No fruit is subsequently produced in some cases where flowering occurs.

l: youth, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: A youth deserves respect because his future may equal the present; if by forty or fifty he has not made himself heard of, he no longer merits such regard.

l: future, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_not_equal_to present [as a possibility concerning a youth] The future of a youth may become equal to the present of those judging him.

l: present, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: The present is used as the standard to which a youth’s future may become equal.

l: respect, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Respect is to be shown to a youth. A youth who has not made himself heard of by forty or fifty will not be worth being regarded with respect.

l: men, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Men may refuse to assent to words of strict admonition or refuse to be pleased with words of gentle advice, according to the Master.

l: words of strict admonition, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_a admonition [strict] Words of strict admonition may receive assent from men. Their value is shown when they reform conduct.

l: conduct, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_reformed_by words of strict admonition [when a man assents to them] Conduct is reformed because of words of strict admonition.

l: words of gentle advice, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_a advice [gentle] Words of gentle advice may please men. Their value is shown when they unfold aim.

l: aim, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_unfolded_by words of gentle advice [when a man is pleased with them] Aim is unfolded through words of gentle advice.

l: a man, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: A man may be pleased with words of gentle advice without unfolding their aim, or assent to words of strict admonition without reforming his conduct. The Master says he can do nothing with such a man.

l: faithfulness, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_a first principle Faithfulness is presented by The Master as a first principle.

l: sincerity, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: is_a first principle Sincerity is presented by The Master as a first principle.

l: friends, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: are_equal_to yourself [as a condition for friendship] The Master advises having no friends who are not equal to oneself.

l: faults, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: are_abandoned when present [without fear] The Master teaches that when a person has faults, the person should not fear abandoning them.

l: commander (of the forces of a large state), The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: A commander commands a large state's forces and, despite that authority, may be carried off.

l: will (of a common man), The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
s: Will, possessed even by a common man, remains inalienable: it cannot be taken from him.

l: a common man, The Analects of Confucius, Book IX (Tsze Han)
